newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: FRANCE REASSURES EUROPE ON SINGLE CURRENCY.
newsitem.headline: FRANCE REASSURES EUROPE ON SINGLE CURRENCY.

text.p: France's finance minister on Sunday reassured his European colleagues that the new government remained committed to a single currency and ministers said they believed an accord could be reached on the most contentious issue -- a stability pact limiting budget deficits.

French Finance Minister Dominque Strauss-Kahn told reporters he "could not see how anyone could have doubted it" when asked whether the new Socialist-led government would stick to the timetable and criteria for launching a single currency on January 1, 1999.
"Mr Strauss-Kahn let us know that the January 1, 1999 date will be respected," Luxembourg Finance Minister Jean-Claude Juncker said after a meeting of EU finance ministers.
Strauss-Kahn declined all comment on the stability pact, limiting budget deficits after the launch of the euro.
It was due to be discussed by European Union finance ministers in Luxembourg on Monday ahead of a approval at an EU summit in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17.
French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, who has pledged to fight austerity in Europe, said during the election campaign he did not feel bound by the pact, agreed in Dublin last year.
But ministers said that they had been reassured that there could be a way to assuage France's fears about the pact without reopening negotiations.
Any attempt to renegotiate the pact could create a diplomatic crisis with Germany, which sees it as a guarantee of fiscal discipline after the launch of the euro in 1999.
"We can find the ways and means to reach an agreement in Amsterdam," Juncker said.
Finnish Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto told reporters he thought the pact would be approved in Amsterdam.
Juncker said the pact was meant to ensure that the values of economic stability were enshrined in EMU.
"We have to see with the stability pact if we can reach an interpretation which suits everybody," he said.

Economists have suggested that France's new government might leave the body of the stability pact intact, but insist on adding some new wording which places the emphasis on fighting for growth and employment.
It could also look for further moves towards a European economic government which would draw up policies for the euro zone designed to boost growth and lower unemployment.

Juncker said that during the Luxembourg presidency of the EU, which starts next month, he would ask social affairs ministers to discuss ways in which they could join finance ministers in defining economic policies for the euro zone.
The social affairs ministers are due to meet informally in July. This could be a way to moving towards "what you call an economic government," he told reporters.

France's previous centre-right government had pushed hard for an economic government, but, facing German resistance, had settled instead for an informal "stability council" to co-ordinate economic policies.

An economic government, acting alongside the future European Central Bank, which involved both finance ministers and social affairs ministers -- thereby stressing the need for economic policies to boost jobs -- was a key demand made by the Socialist party during the election campaign.
